assumptions: The founder will not fund receivables from personal capital or present the service as a lender without the required authorization.
The family installation firm participates only through explicit opt-in and lawful beneficiary consent.
At least one form of installer or beneficiary payment right can be financed under a compliant Polish structure.
No receivable origination right, funder commitment, underwriting terms, or paying installer is currently secured.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A Polish legal opinion on the exact payment right and intermediation model, a funder's written term sheet and data requirements, opt-in installer files showing gap duration and size, approval and rejection outcomes, loss assumptions, and observed willingness to pay.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The proposal identifies a specific staged cash-flow gap created by partial prefinancing and post-completion documentation, then separates verification and origination from balance-sheet lending by the founder.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Material and payroll outflows before final subsidy payment can constrain installers and delay jobs, but actual delay, advance size, rejection loss, and willingness to pay either a verification or success fee are not measured.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Origination and verification fees can be capital-light and repeat with project flow, but lawful fee structure, funder pricing, approval rate, recourse, fraud review, manual exceptions, acquisition cost, and cash conversion remain unknown.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Small Polish Clean Air installers constitute a precise initial segment and the family firm may support a bounded workflow test, but eligible financing volume, geographic density, and the share with an acute funding gap are unquantified.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Program-specific normalization and multi-funder routing could form a useful wedge, but banks, factors, distributors, operators, and vertical brokers can internalize intake and control the capital or customer relationship.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A trusted verification and funding rail could extend to more installers, funders, retrofit programs, and other documented trade receivables, although each program introduces bespoke rights and underwriting rules.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Permissioned defect, timing, approval, and repayment outcomes plus a multi-funder network could compound, but transaction rights are not secured and program changes can rapidly obsolete specialized workflows.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: The founder's finance and data skills fit document-risk triage, and an opt-in family installer could provide unusually practical workflow access, though it supplies neither a lender commitment nor transferable beneficiary rights.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Current partial-prefinancing rules and a longer completion window expose a timely cash-conversion problem, while the same dependence on changing public-program rules makes the opportunity fragile.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Accountants, distributors, contractor groups, advisers, and licensed funders can reach installers at the financing trigger, but no channel or funding partner has agreed to originate or fund cases.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A document-readiness pilot is feasible without founder lending, but assignability, beneficiary consent, credit-intermediation boundaries, AML, fraud, lender underwriting, and external funding are threshold dependencies rather than ordinary product details.

highest_value_structural_change: Make the first product a paid document-readiness and lender-routing pilot with one installer and one licensed funder, adding transaction exclusivity only after the funder defines an accepted, legally reviewed receivable structure.
main_structural_strength: A concrete program-induced working-capital gap can be converted into a repeatable verification event while external licensed partners, rather than the founder, supply capital.
primary_score_limiter: The proposed paid transaction may fail at the legal and capital-provider layer because subsidy eligibility does not establish assignability, collateral value, or funder appetite.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The program already provides partial prefinancing and free operator support, while an eligible, well-documented project is not necessarily an assignable or fundable receivable.
